content: For malaria prevention in younger children, national malaria programs may consider implementing Intermittent Preventive Treatment for school-aged children (IPTsc). Most studies on IPTsc have focused on children under 15 years of age. Evidence suggests that the intervention may have a stronger impact on malaria-related anemia in children under 10 years compared to those aged 10–15 years. However, the effect of IPTsc on Plasmodium falciparum infection appears consistent across these age groups. If older children are included in IPTsc programs, special attention should be given to how girls who have reached menarche are managed, as certain antimalarial drugs should not be administered without confirming pregnancy status. There is limited data on the safety, efficacy, and pharmacokinetics of most antimalarial drugs during pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester. In studies involving girls with a history of menarche, pregnancy status was determined through self-reporting or pregnancy tests. Further research is needed to safely include girls of reproductive age in IPTsc programs. Dosage and Administration School-aged children should receive a full course of antimalarial drugs at the recommended treatment dose for IPTsc. Dosage should ideally be based on the child’s weight, with age-based dosing used only when weight cannot be determined. The frequency of IPTsc administration should be guided by local malaria epidemiology, including transmission intensity and seasonality, as well as the pharmacokinetics of the chosen drug and the feasibility of delivering additional courses. IPTsc should be timed to provide protection during periods of highest malaria risk. Most trials have administered IPTsc either monthly or each school term. In areas with perennial malaria transmission, higher transmission intensity may necessitate the use of drugs with longer half-lives or more frequent dosing to maximize protection. If year-round IPTsc is not feasible due to resource constraints, it should be targeted to peak transmission periods. Delivery Approaches IPTsc can be delivered through schools or community-based approaches. The delivery method should consider local malaria epidemiology and whether school-based delivery aligns with peak malaria risk periods. All schools serving children up to 15 years in the target area should be included. National malaria programs may collaborate with existing health initiatives targeting school-aged children to facilitate IPTsc delivery. Special efforts may be needed to reach children not attending school, as they are often at higher risk of malaria. In areas with seasonal transmission, community-based approaches may be more appropriate if school schedules do not align with peak transmission periods. If older age groups are included, communication strategies should address the inclusion of girls of reproductive age. Drug Resistance The impact of drug resistance on IPTsc efficacy is not fully understood. A re-analysis of data on resistance markers following monthly IPTsc with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-P) found no evidence of increased resistance markers. Current evidence suggests that malaria chemoprevention, as implemented to date, does not inevitably lead to increased resistance, and even high resistance rates may not necessarily impair chemoprevention efficacy. However, expanded use of antimalarial drugs could increase resistance over time. Strategies such as using different drugs for chemoprevention and treatment, or combining drugs with complementary resistance mechanisms, may help preserve efficacy. Special Populations Children with sickle cell disease should be included in IPTsc unless they are already receiving regular chemoprevention for their condition. Co-delivery of IPTsc with other school health programs should follow drug manufacturers’ guidance on safety and contraindications. Girls of reproductive age should not receive certain antimalarials for prophylaxis without confirming they are not pregnant. IPTsc is not recommended for children with severe acute illness, those unable to take oral medication, those who have received a dose of the IPTsc drug within the past 30 days, or those allergic to the drugs used. IPTsc with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) should not be given to individuals receiving sulfa-based medications, such as co-trimoxazole for HIV. Acceptability and Feasibility Community sensitization is critical for improving the acceptability of IPTsc. Studies have shown high willingness among children to take IPTsc tablets, and parents generally view the intervention as useful. However, side effects from the drugs may reduce acceptance, particularly for subsequent treatment rounds. Simpler antimalarial regimens, such as single-dose treatments, may enhance compliance. School-based delivery is likely more feasible than community-based approaches, but absenteeism and low school enrollment could limit reach. In some countries, schools already serve as platforms for health interventions, such as nutrition programs and insecticide-treated net distribution, which could facilitate IPTsc implementation. Cost and Cost-Effectiveness The cost of IPTsc varies depending on the drug regimen and delivery method. Key cost drivers include human resources (e.g., training teachers) and the cost of the drugs. IPTsc is likely to be cost-effective, particularly in areas where school-aged children are at high risk of malaria during the school term. Integrating IPTsc with existing school health programs could yield cost savings. Equity Considerations Delivering IPTsc solely through schools may affect equity, as children not attending school are often from lower socioeconomic groups and are at higher malaria risk. There is some evidence that the impact of IPTsc on school performance may differ between boys and girls. Research Needs Further research is needed to address evidence gaps, including the optimal frequency of IPTsc administration, the cost-effectiveness of combining IPTsc with other school health programs, and the development of single-dose antimalarial drugs for chemoprevention. Studies should also explore the impact of IPTsc on cognition, school performance, and community-level malaria transmission, as well as strategies to safely include girls of reproductive age. Post-Discharge Malaria Chemoprevention (PDMC) PDMC involves administering a full course of antimalarial treatment at regular intervals to children admitted with severe anemia, aiming to prevent new malaria infections during the high-risk post-discharge period. PDMC should be provided even when the cause of severe anemia cannot be identified. Drugs used for PDMC can include first-line malaria treatments, but alternative medicines are preferred. The frequency of PDMC administration should be guided by the protective efficacy of the selected drug, the duration of the transmission season, and the feasibility of delivering additional treatments. Delivery strategies for PDMC include community-based and facility-based approaches, with community-based delivery showing higher adherence rates. Implementation and Monitoring The safety and impact of IPTsc programs should be routinely monitored using hospital, clinic, and community health worker data. School surveys can evaluate outcomes related to school attendance and achievement. Molecular markers associated with drug resistance should be analyzed cautiously to monitor the potential spread of resistance. A guide to support IPTsc implementation and a manual for tailoring malaria interventions at the subnational level are under development. Conclusion The WHO recommends a conditional implementation of IPTsc for school-aged children in moderate to high malaria transmission settings, given its moderate benefits and minimal undesirable effects.
